newsitem.title: USA: Mozambique gets IMF cash, HIPC loan deal closer.
newsitem.headline: Mozambique gets IMF cash, HIPC loan deal closer.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund approved a $35 million loan for Mozambique on Tuesday and said a decision to let Russia join the Paris Club of creditor states could help Mozambique win large-scale debt relief.

An IMF statement said reformist Mozambique was a strong candidate for the Highly Indebted Poor Countries (HIPC) initiative -- an international programme under which Paris Club members agree to cooperate to ease a country's debt burden.
The initiative is open only to countries that have made good progress on market-oriented economic reforms.

"Mozambique's economic performance since 1996 has been commendable, thanks to the government's persistence with strong economic reforms," the statement said, noting that the Maputo had met the aims of the IMF's 1996-97 loan programme.

"The government carried out a number of structural reforms, including the privatisation of the Commercial Bank of Mozambique, a reform of the customs duty and consumption tax structures, creation of an interbank market for foreign exchange and the reduction of import barriers."
The IMF programme for 1997/98 envisages GDP growth of 6 percent this year and 11.6 percent in 1998, after 6.4 percent in 1996 and 1.5 percent in 1995.
Inflation is set to fall to 14 percent in 1997 and 10 percent in 1998, from 16.6 percent last year.

IMF economists have long expressed satisfaction with the Mozambique economic reform programme, but the fact that most of its foreign debts were to non Paris Club member Russia made it difficult for it to reap the benefits of the HIPC programme.
But Russia, which inherited responsibility for both the debts and the liabilities of the former Soviet Union, won agreement in principle to join the Paris Club as a creditor.

Moscow officials said during last weekend's Denver summit of world leaders that this had sealed Russia's full entry to the world economic community and increased the possibility that some of the Soviet-era loans would be repaid.

The credits, denominated in now-defunct convertible roubles, were extended to Soviet allies in the communist bloc and in the developing world, but more for reasons of political expediency than with any thought of how they could be repaid.
